transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-09
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Jordan Liu (SE), Alex Rivera (Product); Samir Khan (CTO - Orion), Lina Morales (ML Engineer), David Park (Security)
Links shared: deck: https://app.redwood/demo-deck (shared), benchmark sheet: https://drive/redwood/benchmarks-orion (note: mock link)

Summary (auto): quick demo of JSON mode + function calling, schema enforcement, and guardrails, with discussion around Dedicated vs Hosted and security needs.

00:00 Speaker 1 (Maya): hey everyone, thanks for joining. I see Samir, Lina, David, hey, thanks for making time. we wanted to run through how Redwood handles structured outputs and function calling \u001f JSON mode, schemas, and the guardrails we use so you get deterministic responses for downstream systems.
00:22 Speaker 2 (Samir): yeah thanks, Maya. high level we need to ensure outputs are machine-parseable, we have to avoid hallucinated fields \u001f also our security team will want to know about egress/PII.
00:35 Speaker 1 (Maya): perfect, that's exactly what we'll hit. Jordan's going to show a live demo in the Console and then Alex will talk about Optimize recommendations and cost/latency tradeoffs.
00:48 Speaker 3 (Jordan): okay jumping in. I'm going to open the Redwood Console, show JSON mode \u001f you can pick a schema that enforces types and required fields \u001f and then I'll demo function-calling where the model selects a tool and we capture structured output.
01:12 Speaker 3 (Jordan): quick note, sometimes the transcriber writes KV cache as 'kay vee cache' \u001f sorry if you see odd text in logs.
01:27 Speaker 2 (Lina): that's fine. on our side we already have a microservice that expects a strict patient-summary JSON, so the schema enforcement is key. latency around 200ms p50 is our goal but cost matters too.
01:41 Speaker 3 (Jordan): got it. here's the Console: on the left you pick model variant, below there's a toggle for JSON mode. we show a sample schema \u001f for example: patientId (string), diagnosisCodes (array string), severity (enum low/medium/high), followUp (boolean) \u001f when JSON mode is on we run a schema validator against the model output and can optionally auto-retry up to N times or apply deterministic reparsing.
02:10 Speaker 3 (Jordan): demo prompt: "Summarize patient note and extract structured follow-up items". hitting run... streaming response comes back, you can see token stream but the Console also renders the parsed JSON. if parsing fails it flags an error and shows the raw output.
02:36 Speaker 4 (Lina): in the failure case do you apply any repair strategies? like do you autocorrect types or call back to the model with an instruction to only output JSON?
02:49 Speaker 3 (Jordan): yes, there are a few options: 1) strict: if parse fails we return an error and mark the request; 2) soft-repair: we call the model with a short repair prompt to re-output valid JSON (we keep a retry budget); 3) function-call fallback where the model calls a tool that enforces structure server-side. you can configure per-route behavior in the API or Console.
03:15 Speaker 1 (Maya): and from a product standpoint, the important piece is observability \u001f we log parsing failures, ratelimit, token counts, and you can filter by prompt type. Alex will show Optimize which can recommend batching/quant profiles to hit your latency/cost targets.
03:33 Speaker 5 (David): security question: when you do function-calling or schema parsing, where does that intermediate data live? is it logged in plaintext or encrypted?
03:44 Speaker 1 (Maya): good question. by default hosted keeps logs for 30 days but you can configure retention; in Dedicated/Private we can disable transcript retention or push logs into your VPC syslog. everything at rest is encrypted with KMS; for Private we support customer-managed keys \u001f H-S-M integrations possible.
04:05 Speaker 5 (David): SOC two?
04:08 Speaker 1 (Maya): SOC 2 Type II \u001f yes, we'll share the report. sometimes the transcriber writes SOC 'two' so you'll see variations.
04:24 Speaker 3 (Jordan): back to demo \u001f now switching to API example. in JSON mode the SDK returns a parsed object if valid and includes a 'parsing_status' field. when using function-calling we declare the function signature (name, params schema) in the call. the model can respond with a function call payload which our runtime maps to the registered function, and we can choose to run the function or just surface the call.
04:56 Speaker 4 (Lina): can you show an example where the model calls a 'create_followup' tool and we have a backend that validates and stores a ticket?
05:07 Speaker 3 (Jordan): sure. demo: define function create_followup({ patientId: string, action: string, dueDate?: string }) \u001f model responds with call: create_followup and params. here we show a pipeline: parse -> dry run (validate against service contract) -> commit. if validation fails we don't commit and we surface the error.
05:39 Speaker 2 (Samir): and what's the latency on that extra validation step? we have tight tail-latency SLOs for our UI flows.
05:48 Speaker 3 (Jordan): depends \u001f synchronous validation inside the request path adds some ms; we recommend async commit for heavier checks or using small micro-batching. Redwood Optimize can suggest batching size to hit p50/p95 targets.
06:05 Speaker 6 (Alex): one thing to call out \u001f Optimize analyzes token distribution and sequence lengths and recommends quantization profiles and batching that preserve accuracy for structured outputs. for example, for schema-heavy extraction you may want FP16 or int8 quant that preserves string fidelity; we surface expected unit-cost delta.
06:34 Speaker 2 (Lina): interesting. are there guardrails to prevent the model from inventing new fields or mis-attributing enums?
06:43 Speaker 3 (Jordan): yes, schemas are first-class. you can define enums and mark fields required. we also have a strict mode where any unknown fields are dropped and counted as a parse error. additionally we support custom validators \u001f regex, length checks \u001f and can pipe parse errors into a replay queue for retraining prompts.
07:10 Speaker 5 (David): from a compliance view, does Redwood store the raw output until we approve? and can that be disabled?
07:20 Speaker 1 (Maya): yes, you can opt-out of storing raw transcripts; for Dedicated/Private you can disable or ship logs to your VPC. we also have RBAC, SSO/SAML, and audit logs for who viewed what.
07:42 Speaker 3 (Jordan): showing Console 'route configs' now \u001f you can route by region, tier, or latency policy. fallback behaviors: if a model variant fails parse repeatedly, we can route to a simpler model or a guarded variant that is quantized differently. this keeps your app online.
08:10 Speaker 2 (Samir): hypothetical: if we need on-prem because of PHI restrictions, what's the deployment cadence and what's the infra footprint?
08:21 Speaker 6 (Alex): Private deployment package is available; typical footprint for our inference nodes is N GPUs per 100 qps depending on model. we can provide sizing guidance; we also do an initial onboarding where we run a baseline benchmark against your sample dataset.
08:42 Speaker 4 (Lina): can the POC run with a hosted pilot first and then move to Dedicated? we want to validate accuracy before committing infra.
08:51 Speaker 1 (Maya): absolutely \u001f common pattern is hosted free credits + small pilot, then Dedicated reserved capacity for production. we can also do a short Dedicated trial with committed capacity.
09:05 Speaker 3 (Jordan): demo: here's a CLI/API snippet. call: redwood.completions.create({ mode: 'json', schema: 'patientFollowUpV1', functions: ['create_followup'], max_retries: 2 }) response: { parsing_status: 'ok', output: { patientId: '12345', followUps: [ { action: 'call patient', dueDate: '2025-10-20' } ] } }
09:36 Speaker 2 (Lina): hmm the sample shows followUps array \u001f we need consistent field names. can we enforce camelCase or snake_case?
09:45 Speaker 3 (Jordan): yep you can set naming conventions in schema normalization; Console can enforce and the SDK will normalize fields on parse.
09:55 Speaker 4 (Lina): what about partial outputs? like model gives some fields and misses required ones \u001f how do you handle partial but usable outputs?
10:05 Speaker 3 (Jordan): we annotate partial parses with 'confidence' and 'missing_fields'. policy options: accept partial with warning, retry to fill missing fields, or escalate to human-in-the-loop.
10:25 Speaker 5 (David): do you maintain an audit trail that ties parsed outputs back to raw model tokens for forensics?
10:33 Speaker 1 (Maya): yes, for customers that need it we maintain an immutable audit trail. for hosted customers this is optional; Dedicated/Private gives more control.
10:46 Speaker 3 (Jordan): demo continues \u001f now showing guardrail templates. you can add a 'no-PHI leakage' rule where the model is constrained to not include certain fields; we can also add post-parse filters that scrub or mask values before returning to the app.
11:12 Speaker 2 (Samir): are post-parse scrubbers configurable per route? we have different teams with different data rules.
11:19 Speaker 3 (Jordan): yes per-route configs. you could have a 'clinical-route' that masks SSNs and a 'billing-route' that allows billing codes.
11:28 Speaker 6 (Alex): Optimize can run evals against a prompt set to surface regressions when switching model variants or quant profiles. we tie quality alerts to your evaluation dataset so you get notified if structured extraction F1 drops.
11:48 Speaker 4 (Lina): that'll be critical; we can't lose extraction fidelity as we optimize for cost.
11:56 Speaker 3 (Jordan): showing an example eval: baseline vs int8 quant model, extraction F1 drops 0.02 \u001f Optimize flags it and recommends alternative quant profile or batching instead.
12:12 Speaker 5 (David): question: for function-calling, where are keys for downstream tools stored? we don't want secrets leaked.
12:22 Speaker 1 (Maya): keys can be stored in your KMS or in Redwood's secret manager with envelope encryption. in Dedicated/Private you can keep keys entirely on-prem.
12:34 Speaker 2 (Samir): what's the fallback if a model starts inventing fields during a rollout? we need fail-closed behavior.
12:44 Speaker 3 (Jordan): you can set model rollouts to canary. if parse error rate spikes above threshold, we auto-fallback to previous model variant and alert. there's a safety net.
13:00 Speaker 4 (Lina): any limits on schema complexity? nested objects etc?
13:08 Speaker 3 (Jordan): we support nested schemas, arrays, maps; the validator supports JSON Schema-like rules and some custom types. deep nesting can increase parse fragility so we recommend denormalizing where possible.
13:26 Speaker 5 (David): timeline: if we do a POC what's realistic? we need to present to legal and security.
13:35 Speaker 1 (Maya): typical POC is 4 weeks: week 1 onboarding + sample data, week 2 run benchmarks, week 3 iterate prompts and guardrails, week 4 finalize metrics. legal/sec review runs in parallel \u001f we can provide security package and data flow diagrams.
13:55 Speaker 3 (Jordan): quick demo of function calling with a tool that queries EHR \u001f model returns a function call, we show a dry run validator that checks permissions. the actual call runs under a service account.
14:20 Speaker 2 (Lina): crosstalk: (inaudible) \u001f sorry missed that last bit.
14:25 Speaker 3 (Jordan): no worries, basically you can require the model to include an 'auth_scope' field and our runtime will validate before executing tool calls.
14:36 Speaker 6 (Alex): also note that Optimize surfaced a case where removing prefix tokens from prompts reduced hallucination on schema fields \u001f it's subtle but it helps.
14:50 Speaker 2 (Samir): one more on billing: how do you charge function-calls or repair retries? we want predictable unit economics.
14:59 Speaker 1 (Maya): billing is token-based for hosted. for retries you can opt to not bill for internal repair calls up to a configured budget during pilot. Dedicated is contract-based with reserved capacity. we can model expected costs given your sample workload.
15:20 Speaker 3 (Jordan): demo wrap-up: you'll get logs: parsed_json, raw_output, parsing_status, model_variant, token_counts. we also showed how to push alerts to Slack and run automated rollback if error rates spike.
15:42 Speaker 2 (Lina): can we test with our sample patient notes?
15:47 Speaker 1 (Maya): yes, we'll provide a benchmark harness. Jordan will run a 1k request run against your sample prompts and share results.
15:55 Speaker 4 (Lina): cool. security: David will need the SOC 2 and data flow.
16:01 Speaker 5 (David): yep, and encryption details and whether transcripts can be disabled.
16:08 Speaker 1 (Maya): we'll include that in the follow-up packet.
16:12 Speaker 3 (Jordan): quick live Q&A: Lina: can we scope a POC that includes both hosted and a small Dedicated slot for head-to-head?
16:22 Speaker 2 (Samir): yes we'd like a side-by-side for accuracy/cost.
16:27 Speaker 1 (Maya): perfect \u001f next steps we'll send pricing and a proposed 4-week POC plan.
16:35 Speaker 6 (Alex): one last note \u001f when you do function-calling with external tools we recommend a validation sandbox so no real PHI leaves during testing.
16:46 Speaker 2 (Lina): agreed.
16:50 Speaker 3 (Jordan): end of demo; quick recap?
16:54 Speaker 1 (Maya): recap: 1) Redwood JSON mode + schemas enforce structured outputs; 2) function calling maps to tools with validation & dry-run; 3) guardrails + post-parse scrubbers for PHI; 4) Optimize recommends cost/quant profiles and detects regressions; 5) next steps: send pricing, security docs, benchmark harness, and schedule POC scoping.
17:20 Speaker 2 (Samir): thanks everyone.
17:22 Speaker 1 (Maya): thanks, we'll follow up with the packet.

Note: transcript contains occasional transcription artifacts (mis-spelled product names, 'SOC two', 'kay vee cache').
